title: Lesson 8: Alpha-Beta Pruning and Modern Game Search

slides.title: Alpha-Beta Pruning and Modern Game Search

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Lesson eight begins with a promise that sounds suspiciously like a late-night advertisement: obtain the same minimax decision while examining less of the tree. Alpha-beta pruning keeps the minimax backup rule, terminal utilities, cutoff depth, and evaluation function. It saves work only when returned values prove that unexplored siblings cannot change an ancestor's choice.

visualDesign.focusPhrase: Lesson eight begins with a promise

focuses.phrase: Lesson eight begins with a promise
focuses.label: Concept framing

segments.label: Mechanism and metaphor
segments.text: Picture a restaurant menu where your opponent has already guaranteed that your table will pay no more than twenty dollars. Discovering a branch whose meal costs at least thirty is enough; the opponent will refuse it. Alpha and beta are those remembered alternatives, and the pruning shears appear only after the arithmetic proves irrelevance.

segments.label: Boundary and proof
segments.text: The four cards establish our contract. The result must be the same minimax action. The mechanism is a pair of path bounds. Efficiency depends on visitation order. Evidence is a trace of every recursive return. A cutoff based on vibes is not pruning; it is merely deleting homework with confidence.

slides.title: Minimax may pursue branches whose values cannot matter

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Depth-limited minimax normally evaluates every reachable leaf at its selected ply limit and backs each value toward the root. That is correct but expensive because the branching factor raises the tree size exponentially. Some leaves are evaluated even after an ancestor has an alternative that makes the entire branch strategically unacceptable.

focuses.phrase: Depth-limited minimax normally evaluates every reachable
focuses.label: Concept framing

segments.label: Mechanism and metaphor
segments.text: Imagine interviewing every applicant after one candidate has already met every requirement and the current branch has failed a mandatory test. More interviews cannot rescue that branch. Alpha-beta turns this administrative common sense into inequalities, but unlike a bored hiring committee, it must preserve the exact minimax answer.

segments.label: Boundary and proof
segments.text: Notice what remains fixed: terminal utility, depth limit, evaluation function, legal moves, and the MAX-MIN backup operators. What changes is depth-first visitation plus the moment at which a bound closes. If any of those controlled ingredients change, a matching answer is no longer evidence that pruning alone caused the saving.

segments.label: Transfer and takeaway
segments.text: The structural insight connects nonadjacent levels. A value discovered below a grandchild can prove that the intermediate choice will never be selected by an ancestor. We do not need the exact values of the skipped leaves; we need only establish that even their best possible influence cannot cross the existing alternative.

slides.title: Alpha rises for MAX; beta falls for MIN

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Alpha is the best value MAX can already guarantee along the active path. It is a lower bound because MAX has an explored alternative worth at least alpha. Beta is the best value MIN can already guarantee, meaning an upper bound on MAX's outcome because MIN can force the result to beta or less.

focuses.phrase: Alpha is the best value MAX
focuses.label: Concept framing

segments.label: Mechanism and metaphor
segments.text: Think of alpha as an elevator that only travels upward and beta as an elevator that only travels downward. Returned child values tighten the decision window from both sides. Nobody presses a reverse button: alpha never decreases, and beta never increases while the current path remains active.

visualDesign.focusPhrase: Think of alpha as an elevator

focuses.phrase: Think of alpha as an elevator
focuses.label: Mechanism and metaphor

segments.label: Boundary and proof
segments.text: The displayed interval says alpha is no greater than any still decision-relevant backed-up value, which is no greater than beta. When alpha meets or exceeds beta, the window has closed. Remaining siblings may contain fascinating numbers, dramatic plot twists, or free snacks, but they cannot alter the ancestor decision.

segments.label: Transfer and takeaway
segments.text: Keep utility from MAX's fixed perspective throughout the tree. MIN does not suddenly call a good score positive for itself and flip the signs unless the representation explicitly uses negamax. In this pseudocode, MAX maximizes one utility scale and MIN minimizes that same scale.

slides.title: Finish a child, return its value, then update the parent

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Alpha-beta is depth-first. It chooses one child, descends until a terminal or cutoff state supplies a value, returns that value to the immediate parent, and only then updates the parent's temporary value and bound. It does not sample every sibling at one level before descending, because incomplete children establish no usable backed-up value.

visualDesign.focusPhrase: Alpha-beta is depth-first. It chooses one

focuses.phrase: Alpha-beta is depth-first. It chooses one
focuses.label: Concept framing

segments.label: Mechanism and metaphor
segments.text: The stack behaves like a set of nested phone calls. The leaf answers its parent; the parent updates its own notes and later calls its parent. A leaf does not shout directly to the root across three unfinished conversations. That shortcut would mix values owned by different decision nodes.

segments.label: Boundary and proof
segments.text: At a terminal state return exact utility. At a depth cutoff return the evaluation function used by ordinary depth-limited minimax. After a MIN child returns, MAX updates v and perhaps alpha. After a MAX child returns, MIN updates v and perhaps beta. Bound updates are consequences of completed evidence.

slides.title: A cutoff says an ancestor already has a better alternative

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: At a MAX node, stop when its temporary value v reaches or exceeds beta. This is a beta cutoff. A MIN ancestor already possesses an alternative that keeps MAX at beta or below, so MIN will never allow the current branch whose MAX value is at least beta.

segments.label: Mechanism and metaphor
segments.text: The family-veto metaphor helps. MAX is excited because this branch offers seven, but the ancestor MIN says, charming story, I can choose another route capped at six. MAX may find nine or ninety among the remaining children; MIN still rejects the branch. The skipped siblings cannot help the root decision.

segments.text: At a MIN node, stop when v falls to or below alpha. This is an alpha cutoff. A MAX ancestor already owns an alternative worth alpha or more, so MAX will never choose a branch where MIN can hold the result to alpha or less. The inequalities mirror the players' preferences.

slides.title: MAX returns as soon as its value reaches beta

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: MAX-VALUE begins with v equal to negative infinity. For each legal action, it recursively asks MIN-VALUE for the child result and replaces v with the larger of its current value and that return. This is ordinary minimax until the upper bound supplied by a MIN ancestor becomes decisive.

segments.label: Mechanism and metaphor
segments.text: Read the return test before the alpha update. If v is at least beta, return v immediately. The remaining children are irrelevant because the MIN ancestor can avoid this branch. Only when the search continues does alpha become the larger of its prior value and v.

segments.label: Boundary and proof
segments.text: The order matters in code and on an exam. First receive the child value, then update v, then test v against beta, then update alpha if another child may be explored. Moving the test before v changes can miss a cutoff; updating the wrong bound can manufacture one from thin air.

segments.text: A useful summary is inequality, owner, consequence. For v at least beta at MAX, a MIN ancestor owns the beta alternative, so remaining MAX siblings are skipped. For v at most alpha at MIN, a MAX ancestor owns the alpha alternative, so remaining MIN siblings are skipped.

segments.label: Boundary and proof
segments.text: Move ordering changes running time because strong early evidence tightens bounds, but it does not change the minimax decision. Expectimax, MCTS, and other extensions answer different modeling needs by changing backup or sampling. Choose them because the environment differs, not because alpha and beta have become unfashionable.

segments.label: Transfer and takeaway
segments.text: Before leaving, identify one operation you can perform without peeking: update bounds, label a cutoff, trace the practice tree, or design a verification test. The durable idea is simple: search may skip work only after completed evidence proves that the skipped work cannot change the chosen action.
